title: Talking to Kids in Spanish: Everyday Phrases for Parents

body_html:
Talking to kids in Spanish is different from talking to adults. You need commands (¡Ponte los zapatos!), praise (¡Muy bien!), comfort, and a lot of tender diminutives. Whether you’re raising bilingual children, visiting family, or helping out with nieces and nephews, these everyday phrases will carry you from breakfast to bedtime. I’ve grouped them by moments of the day, the way you’ll actually use them.

Key takeaways
  • Use tú commands with children: ven, siéntate, lávate las manos.
  • Diminutives add warmth: un ratito, la camita, mi niño.
  • Praise often and specifically: ¡Qué bien lo has hecho!
  • Consistency matters more than perfect grammar for bilingual kids.
{{toc}}

Talking to kids in Spanish: mornings

  • ¡Buenos días, cariño! ¡Arriba! Good morning, sweetheart! Up you get!
  • Es hora de levantarse. It’s time to get up.
  • Vístete, que llegamos tarde. Get dressed, we’re going to be late.
  • Ponte los zapatos / el abrigo. Put your shoes / coat on.
  • Lávate los dientes. Brush your teeth.
  • Agarra la mochila. Grab your backpack. (In Spain: Coge la mochila; see {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}} for why not to use coger in Latin America.)

Mealtimes

  • ¡A comer! Food’s ready! / Time to eat!
  • Lávate las manos antes de comer. Wash your hands before eating.
  • Siéntate bien. Sit properly.
  • Pruébalo, aunque sea un poquito. Try it, even just a little.
  • ¿Quieres más? Do you want more?
  • Cómetelo todo. Eat it all up.

Play and outings

  • ¿A qué jugamos? What shall we play?
  • Te toca a ti. It’s your turn. (see {{link:tocar-vs-jugar|tocar vs jugar}})
  • Vamos al parque. Let’s go to the park.
  • Dame la mano para cruzar. Hold my hand to cross.
  • ¡Cuidado! Careful!
  • Recoge los juguetes. Tidy up your toys.
{{image:2}}

Praise and encouragement

  • ¡Muy bien! Very good!
  • ¡Qué bien lo has hecho! You did that so well!
  • Estoy muy orgulloso/a de ti. I’m very proud of you.
  • ¡Tú puedes! You can do it!
  • Inténtalo otra vez. Try again.
  • ¡Qué listo/a eres! You’re so clever!

Setting limits

  • No, eso no se hace. No, we don’t do that.
  • Para, por favor. Stop, please.
  • Habla más bajito. Speak more quietly.
  • Comparte con tu hermano. Share with your brother.
  • Cuento hasta tres: uno, dos… I’ll count to three: one, two…
  • Pide perdón. Say sorry.
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Comfort and feelings

  • ¿Qué te pasa, mi amor? What’s wrong, love?
  • ¿Dónde te duele? Where does it hurt?
  • Ya pasó, ya pasó. There, there, it’s over.
  • Sana, sana, colita de rana… A traditional rhyme to soothe small bumps.
  • Ven aquí, te doy un abrazo. Come here, I’ll give you a hug.

More comforting phrases in {{link:how-to-comfort-someone-in-spanish|how to comfort someone in Spanish}}.

Bedtime

  • ¡A la cama! / ¡A dormir! Bedtime!
  • Ponte el pijama. Put your pajamas on.
  • ¿Te leo un cuento? Shall I read you a story?
  • Buenas noches, que sueñes con los angelitos. Good night, sweet dreams (literally “dream of little angels”).
  • Te quiero mucho. I love you very much.

Bedtime stories are also a wonderful way to keep Spanish alive at home; see {{link:raising-bilingual-children-english-spanish|raising bilingual children in English and Spanish}} and {{link:bilingual-books-english-spanish|bilingual books in English and Spanish}}.

The magic of diminutives

Spanish speakers add -ito or -ita to soften words when talking to children: un momentito, la camita, el perrito, agüita. It signals tenderness and makes instructions gentler. The RAE dictionary describes -ito as a suffix with diminutive or affectionate value.

A sample morning

  • Parent: ¡Buenos días, mi vida! ¿Has dormido bien?
  • Child: Sí… pero tengo sueño. (Yes… but I’m sleepy.)
  • Parent: Ándale, a desayunar. Hay hotcakes. (Come on, breakfast. There are pancakes.)
  • Child: ¡Bien! (Yay!)

Questions to ask kids

  • ¿Cómo te fue en la escuela? How was school?
  • ¿Qué has aprendido hoy? What did you learn today?
  • ¿Con quién has jugado? Who did you play with?
  • ¿Qué es lo que más te ha gustado del día? What did you like best today?
  • ¿Tienes hambre? ¿Tienes sueño? Are you hungry? Are you sleepy?

Open questions like these get children talking, which is exactly what builds their Spanish.

Tips for bilingual families

If you’re raising children with both English and Spanish, consistency is more important than perfection. Many families use “one parent, one language”, where each parent speaks one language to the children; others use Spanish at home and English outside. Whatever you choose, keep it predictable, read together in Spanish, and celebrate every word your child says in it. Don’t worry if they answer in English for a while; understanding usually comes first and speaking follows. Visits to Spanish-speaking relatives, songs, cartoons and video calls with grandparents all add the real-life input that makes the language stick.

Regional words

Some everyday words change by country: a pacifier is el chupete in Spain and el chupón in Mexico; a diaper is el pañal everywhere; school is el cole in Spain and la escuela or el colegio in Latin America; and a baby’s bottle is el biberón in Spain but la mamadera in Argentina and Chile or el tetero in Colombia.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetterWhy
Ponga sus zapatos.Ponte los zapatos.Tú with children; article for clothes
Lava tus manos.Lávate las manos.Reflexive + article
¡Bueno trabajo!¡Buen trabajo! / ¡Muy bien!Buen before masculine nouns
Es tiempo de dormir.Es hora de dormir.Clock time: hora
{{image:3}}

Final thoughts

Children don’t need perfect Spanish; they need lots of it, delivered with warmth. Use simple commands, praise generously, add diminutives and finish every day with Te quiero mucho. For more everyday phrases, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you tell a child to go to bed in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡A la cama! or ¡A dormir! You can soften it with Venga, cariño, es hora de dormir.

faq.q: How do you praise a child in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Muy bien!, ¡Qué bien lo has hecho!, Estoy muy orgulloso/a de ti or ¡Tú puedes!

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted with children?
faq.a: Tú. Children are always addressed with tú, and parents use tú commands: ven, siéntate, lávate las manos.
